title: DeMuth v. Miller
lead: Daniel Miller’s employer dismissed him after he appeared on television representing a gay and lesbian coalition, then demanded payment when clients followed Miller to a competing practice. The appeal divided the judges over whether enforcing that payment judicially supported the discriminatory dismissal.

actors.name: Donald DeMuth
actors.role: Accounting employer and plaintiff seeking a contractual payment for transferred clients.

actors.name: Daniel Miller
actors.role: Former employee who opened a competing consulting practice.

actors.name: Judge Popovich
actors.role: Author announcing affirmance and offering one enforcement rationale.

actors.name: Judge Olszewski
actors.role: Judge concurring in the result on a different state-action rationale.

actors.name: Judge Johnson
actors.role: Judge agreeing on renewal and preservation but dissenting from enforcement.

proceedings: A jury found the contract continued by conduct and awarded damages molded to $110,000; a wrongful-discharge counterclaim ended in nonsuit. The Superior Court affirmed, 2–1, with the two affirming judges using different constitutional reasoning.
limits: This reports the 1995 decision and its historical authorities, not current employment or constitutional law. Ordinary penalty and restraint objections were waived rather than rejected on their merits. The judges’ competing descriptions of the dismissal are attributed, and the opinion does not separately resolve every counterclaim.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: An accounting relationship develops into employment under annual terms
sections.cue: What did the contested competition provision require?
paragraphs: Donald DeMuth hired Daniel Miller in December 1985 as an independent contractor performing accounting work. Miller became an employee and professional management consultant in May 1986, signing for June 1, 1986 through May 31, 1987. Their work continued through later fiscal years, but signed contracts could be produced for only two. DeMuth recalled witnessing a later signing whose copy could not be found; Miller denied signing after the 1988–1989 term.

Paragraph 8, called a contingent note payable, applied if Miller left or was terminated for cause and established a consulting or accounting business within fifty miles of a current or former client during the next five years. For each client of DeMuth who retained Miller, he would owe 125 percent of the preceding year’s charges. The definition of cause expressly included homosexuality alongside other listed grounds.

Popovich later described that clause as appearing in contracts other than the 1986 agreement; Johnson described the annual writings more generally. The operative clause and its disputed continuation, rather than that difference in historical recital, drove the appeal.

sections.title: Dismissal is followed by competition and a demand for payment
sections.cue: How did the judges characterize the underlying reason differently?
paragraphs: On October 17, 1990, DeMuth dismissed Miller after a television appearance representing a gay and lesbian coalition. Miller then formed a competing consulting practice and solicited clients; seventeen moved their business from DeMuth to Miller. DeMuth demanded the contractual payment.

Popovich’s opinion later characterized the dismissal in terms of the public appearance, possible client reactions, and sexual orientation. Johnson, relying on trial admissions, insisted that DeMuth discharged Miller because of his acknowledged homosexuality, not any workplace sexual conduct. Their descriptions were part of the judicial disagreement, not one undisputed finding adopted by the entire panel.

sections.title: The contract suit produces a verdict and a disputed continuation finding
sections.cue: Which claims and trial rulings reached the appeal?
paragraphs: DeMuth sued for breach of contract and misappropriation of property rights, initially seeking more than $120,000. Miller denied a governing written contract for the final employment year and asserted that the homosexuality provision violated public policy. He counterclaimed for wrongful discharge, defamation concerning sexuality and AIDS risk, and interference with clients. Johnson’s separate opinion also reported letters from DeMuth suggesting former clients obtain an HIV test if they contemplated continuing interaction with Miller.

Miller sought to exclude continuation evidence because paragraph 5 of the complaint said the agreement was not renewed or extended after May 31, 1990. The trial judge permitted evidence of subsequent conduct. The parties stipulated that damages under the formula did not exceed $110,000. The court entered a compulsory nonsuit on wrongful discharge.

Through special interrogatories, the jury found the parties remained contractually bound by their conduct and awarded damages later molded to $110,000. Miller appealed after denial of relevant requests for judgment notwithstanding the verdict or a new trial. The appellate opinion did not separately adjudicate every counterclaim.

sections.title: All three judges permit the jury to consider renewal by conduct
sections.cue: Why was the complaint sentence not a conclusive admission?
paragraphs: The panel agreed that the alleged judicial admission failed. Under the doctrine applied, a binding admission was an express factual concession for the party’s advantage. The nonrenewal sentence had to be read with allegations of continued work, pay, benefits, termination for contractually specified cause, and paragraph-8 compensation. Reading it to extinguish all terms would defeat, not advance, DeMuth’s pleaded case.

Continued work after a fixed term, without objection or a new arrangement, could imply continuation on prior conditions. Miller kept working and received pay and benefits; his salary increased from $32,500 to $50,000. Both parties described formal renewals occurring four or five months into a fiscal year, with retroactive raises. They resolved a bonus dispute in February 1990 and paid the bonus. Those facts supported a jury question despite the missing signed copy.

sections.title: Different preservation rulings separate the contractual and constitutional objections
sections.cue: What was not decided on its merits?
paragraphs: Miller’s argument that the payment was an unlawful penalty or unreasonable restrictive covenant had not appeared in pretrial, trial, or post-trial motions, and the trial court had not decided it. The appellate court treated that challenge as waived. Affirmance therefore did not substantively establish that every five-year, fifty-mile, 125-percent provision was reasonable.

Public-policy and constitutional objections received different treatment. Though absent from relevant earlier submissions, they appeared in a later supporting brief and oral argument, and the trial judge chose to address them. Under the preservation approach then applied, Popovich reviewed them because the lower court had actually decided them. That did not cure the separate waiver of penalty and reasonableness arguments.

sections.title: Popovich views the payment as compensation for later competition
paragraphs: Popovich distinguished the completed dismissal, which Miller disclaimed directly challenging on this appeal, from the suit over seventeen clients moving to his practice. In Popovich’s view, the judgment enforced a competition-related obligation rather than imposing payment simply because Miller was gay. The general restraint objection remained waived.

He rejected the presented state and federal constitutional and public-policy claims. His account emphasized the televised appearance, client reactions, and nondisclosure of sexual orientation, and regarded the particular claim as nonactionable under the invoked law. His discussion of Shelley, the judicial-enforcement precedent, and employment-property doctrines distinguished a challenge to the payment provision from a direct claim to continued employment. He directed broader employment-policy change toward the legislature and emphasized the record and framing. Those propositions were his historical reasoning, not the reasoning adopted by both judges voting to affirm.

sections.title: Olszewski avoids the constitutional merits by finding no state action here
sections.cue: Why did he concur only through a narrower rationale?
paragraphs: Judge Olszewski agreed with the first two issues and the result but declined to decide whether sexual-orientation discrimination violated equal protection. He found no governmental action in enforcement of this particular competition promise.

He distinguished courts coercing discriminatory employment or directly ordering payment because of status from compensation for later competition. Acknowledging the rule against judicial support of private bias reflected in Shelley and Barrows, he warned that enforcing every private agreement could not automatically become state action.

For Olszewski, the dismissal was already complete and unchallenged, and paragraph 8 could have been activated by numerous defined causes. The court enforced a separate economic consequence without itself deciding whether homosexuality constituted cause. If the contract had not specified that ground and a court had to create it, a different question might arise. He therefore saw no need for Popovich’s constitutional merits discussion.

sections.title: Johnson sees judicial enforcement of a discriminatory trigger
sections.cue: Why would he have entered judgment for Miller?
paragraphs: Judge Johnson agreed on renewal and the first two appellate issues but rejected separating the payment from the cause-based dismissal activating it. DeMuth sought judicial coercion to profit from that trigger. Under Shelley and Barrows, consent to a private agreement did not prevent its judicial enforcement from being state action.

Johnson found no need to decide whether heightened scrutiny applied. He considered enforcement irrational even under rational-basis review: the record showed capable work and partnership prospects, no work-related sexual conduct, and dismissal based on status. Prejudice or anticipated client prejudice offered no legitimate reason for judicial enforcement. He distinguished national-security and conduct cases and explained why the then-existing Bowers privacy decision about a sodomy statute did not resolve this equal-protection claim.

He also rejected dependence on legislative or social consensus. Constitutional protection did not await consensus, and executive and municipal employment protections offered contrary policy evidence. Johnson would reverse and order judgment notwithstanding the verdict for Miller.

sections.title: The damages judgment stands through two different affirming views
paragraphs: After argument June 21, 1994, the Pennsylvania Superior Court decided the appeal January 11, 1995. The $110,000 judgment was affirmed, with Popovich and Olszewski supporting the result and Johnson dissenting from enforcement.

The common conclusions on continuation and preservation did not make Popovich’s entire constitutional discussion a panel-majority rationale. The decision’s outcome and its divided explanations must remain distinct.
